valid-palindrome.pattern: Two pointers moving inwards from both ends

approaches.name: Clean a copy, then compare it with its reverse
approaches.idea: Build the string the question actually talks about (only letters and digits, lower-cased) and check it against its reverse.
steps: Walk through `s` and append every letter or digit, lower-cased, to a builder.
Make a reversed copy of the cleaned string.
The answer is whether the cleaned string equals its reverse.
approaches.why: One pass to clean, one to reverse and one to compare: O(n) time. The cleaned copy and its reverse take O(n) extra memory.

approaches.name: Two pointers that skip what does not count
approaches.idea: Compare the string from both ends at once, skipping characters that are not letters or digits, so no copy is needed.
steps: Put `i` at the first character and `j` at the last.
While `i < j`: if `s[i]` is not a letter or digit, move `i` right; if `s[j]` is not, move `j` left.
Otherwise compare the two characters lower-cased. If they differ, return false; if they match, move both pointers inwards.
If the pointers meet without a mismatch, return true.
approaches.why: Every step moves at least one pointer towards the other, so there are at most n steps. Only two indices are stored.

approaches.name: Collect the distinct values, then copy them back
approaches.idea: Gather each value once in a separate list (the array is sorted, so a value is new when it differs from the last one kept), then write that list over the front of the array.
steps: Create an empty list `unique`.
For each value in `nums`, append it if `unique` is empty or its last element is different.
Copy `unique` into the first positions of `nums`.
Return the size of `unique`.
approaches.why: Two linear passes. The extra list can hold all n values when they are all different, so O(n) memory, which the in-place requirement rules out.

approaches.name: A write pointer behind the read pointer
approaches.idea: The front of the array is the output. A write index `w` marks where the next distinct value goes; because the array is sorted, a value is new exactly when it differs from the last value written.
steps: Start with `w = 0`.
Read every value `x` from left to right.
If `w == 0` or `nums[w - 1] != x`, write `x` at `nums[w]` and increase `w`.
Return `w`; the first `w` slots hold the distinct values in order.
approaches.why: One pass over the array, and `w` never passes the read position, so writes never overwrite a value that is still to be read. Only one index is stored.

move-zeroes.pattern: Read and write pointers (stable partition in place)

approaches.name: Copy the non-zeros into a new array
approaches.idea: Build the answer in a second array (non-zeros first, in order, then zeros) and copy it back.
steps: Create an array `out` of the same length, filled with zeros.
Copy each non-zero value of `nums` into the next free slot of `out`.
The remaining slots of `out` are already 0.
Copy `out` back into `nums`.
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the second array costs O(n) memory, which the in-place requirement forbids.

approaches.name: Write the non-zeros forward, then fill with zeros
approaches.idea: Use the front of the same array as the output: a write index collects non-zeros in order, and everything after it becomes 0.
steps: Set `w = 0`.
For each value `x`, if it is not 0, write it to `nums[w]` and increase `w`.
Set every position from `w` to the end to 0.
approaches.why: Two passes at most, no extra array. It may write zeros over positions that were already zero, which the one-pass swap below avoids.

approaches.name: One pass, swapping each non-zero forward
approaches.idea: Keep the invariant that `nums[0..w)` holds the non-zeros seen so far and `nums[w..i)` holds only zeros. A non-zero at `i` swaps with the first zero at `w`.
steps: Set `w = 0`.
For `i` from 0 to n − 1: if `nums[i] != 0`, swap `nums[i]` and `nums[w]`, then increase `w`.
When the loop ends, all non-zeros are at the front in their original order and the zeros are behind them.
approaches.why: A single pass with constant extra memory. Each element is written at most twice, and an array with few zeros needs few real moves.

squares-of-a-sorted-array.pattern: Two pointers from both ends, filling the output from the back

approaches.name: Square everything, then sort
approaches.idea: Squaring breaks the order (negatives become large), so square each value and sort the result.
steps: Create `out` with `out[i] = nums[i] * nums[i]`.
Sort `out` in ascending order.
Return `out`.
approaches.why: Squaring is O(n); the sort dominates at O(n log n). The output array is O(n) (plus the sort's own stack).

approaches.name: Two pointers, largest square first
approaches.idea: In a sorted array the largest square is always at one of the two ends (the most negative or the most positive value). Take the bigger end each time and fill the output from the back.
steps: Set `i = 0`, `j = n − 1`, and fill position `w` from n − 1 down to 0.
Compare `|nums[i]|` and `|nums[j]|`.
Write the square of the larger one at `out[w]` and move that pointer inwards.
Repeat until `w` passes 0; `out` is sorted ascending.
approaches.why: Each step places one value, so n steps. The output array is required by the problem; besides it only three indices are used, O(1) extra.

two-sum-ii-input-array-is-sorted.pattern: Two pointers on a sorted array (shrink from the side that is too big or too small)

approaches.name: Try every pair
approaches.idea: Check every pair of positions and return the first one that adds up to the target.
steps: For each `i` from 0 to n − 1, and each `j` from `i + 1` to n − 1:
If `numbers[i] + numbers[j] == target`, return `[i + 1, j + 1]` (positions count from 1).
approaches.why: There are n(n − 1)/2 pairs. It ignores the fact that the array is sorted.

approaches.name: Binary search for the partner
approaches.idea: For each value, the partner it needs is `target − numbers[i]`. The array is sorted, so binary search for it to the right of `i`.
steps: For each `i`, let `need = target − numbers[i]`.
Binary search `need` in `numbers[i + 1 .. n − 1]`.
If found at `j`, return `[i + 1, j + 1]`.
approaches.why: n binary searches of O(log n) each. Searching only to the right of `i` avoids using the same element twice.

approaches.name: Two pointers from both ends
approaches.idea: Start with the smallest and the largest value. If their sum is too small, only a bigger left value can help; if it is too big, only a smaller right value can. Each step rules out one value for good.
steps: Set `i = 0` and `j = n − 1`.
While `i < j`, compute `sum = numbers[i] + numbers[j]`.
If `sum == target`, return `[i + 1, j + 1]`.
If `sum < target`, move `i` right; otherwise move `j` left.
approaches.why: Each step moves one pointer, so at most n − 1 steps. When `sum < target`, `numbers[i]` cannot pair with anything at or left of `j` (those are all ≤ `numbers[j]`), so dropping it is safe; the other case is symmetric.

container-with-most-water.pattern: Two pointers from both ends (move the shorter wall)

approaches.name: Try every pair of lines
approaches.idea: The water between lines `i` and `j` is `min(height[i], height[j]) × (j − i)`. Compute it for every pair and keep the largest.
steps: Set `best = 0`.
For every pair `i < j`, compute `min(height[i], height[j]) * (j - i)`.
Keep the maximum in `best` and return it.
approaches.why: n(n − 1)/2 pairs, each O(1). With n up to 10⁵ that is about 5 × 10⁹ operations — too slow.

approaches.name: Two pointers, always moving the shorter line
approaches.idea: Start with the widest container. The shorter wall limits the water; keeping it and moving the taller wall inwards can only lose width without raising the level, so the shorter wall can be discarded.
steps: While `i < j`: update `best` with `min(height[i], height[j]) * (j - i)`.
Move the pointer at the shorter line inwards (either one if they are equal).
Return `best`.
approaches.why: Each step discards one line, so n − 1 steps. Discarding the shorter line is safe: every container still using it has smaller width and a level no higher than that line.

3sum.pattern: Sort, fix one value, then two pointers on the rest (k-sum reduction)

approaches.name: Three nested loops and a set of sorted triplets
approaches.idea: Try every triple of positions. Sorting the array first means each triplet comes out in ascending order, so a set removes repeats.
steps: Sort `nums`.
For every `i < j < k`, if `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`, add the triplet to a set.
Return the contents of the set as a list.
approaches.why: There are about n³/6 triples. The set holds the t distinct answers.

approaches.name: Fix one value, find pairs with a hash set
approaches.idea: With `nums[i]` fixed, the other two must sum to `−nums[i]`: that is Two Sum, which a hash set solves in one pass. Sorting keeps triplets in order so a set can drop repeats.
steps: Sort `nums`.
For each `i`, skip it if `nums[i]` equals `nums[i − 1]` (same first value, same answers).
Walk `j` from `i + 1` with an empty set `seen`: if `−nums[i] − nums[j]` is in `seen`, record the triplet; then add `nums[j]` to `seen`.
Store triplets in a set to drop repeats, and return them.
approaches.why: n choices of `i`, each with an O(n) Two Sum pass. The `seen` set holds up to n values.

approaches.name: Sort, fix one value, two pointers for the other two
approaches.idea: After sorting, fix `nums[i]` and look for a pair summing to `−nums[i]` in the part to its right with two pointers. Skipping equal neighbours removes duplicates without any set.
steps: Sort `nums`. For each `i` (skipping `nums[i] == nums[i − 1]`), set `l = i + 1`, `r = n − 1`.
While `l < r`, compute `sum = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]`.
If `sum < 0`, move `l` right; if `sum > 0`, move `r` left.
If `sum == 0`, record the triplet, then move `l` past every copy of `nums[l]` and `r` past every copy of `nums[r]`, and step both inwards.
Return the collected triplets.
approaches.why: Sorting is O(n log n); each fixed `i` runs an O(n) two-pointer scan, giving O(n²). Apart from the output and the sort's own space, only a few indices are used.

sort-colors.pattern: Three-way partition (Dutch national flag) with three pointers

approaches.name: Use a general sort
approaches.idea: Any comparison sort puts 0s, 1s and 2s in order. It works, but the problem asks you not to use the library sort, and it ignores that there are only three values.
steps: Sort `nums` in place with the language's sort.
The values are only 0, 1 and 2, so the sorted array is exactly the colours grouped in order.
approaches.why: A comparison sort costs O(n log n); library sorts use O(log n) stack (or more for merge-based sorts).

approaches.name: Count each colour, then overwrite (two passes)
approaches.idea: With only three possible values, counting how many of each there are is enough to rebuild the array (counting sort).
steps: Count the 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass.
Overwrite the array: `count[0]` zeros, then `count[1]` ones, then `count[2]` twos.
approaches.why: Two linear passes and a fixed array of 3 counters. It needs two passes, while the problem asks for one.

approaches.name: Dutch national flag: low, mid and high pointers
approaches.idea: Keep three regions: `[0, lo)` all 0s, `[lo, mid)` all 1s, `(hi, n − 1]` all 2s, with `[mid, hi]` still unknown. Look at `nums[mid]` and grow the right region.
steps: Set `lo = 0`, `mid = 0`, `hi = n − 1`.
While `mid <= hi`: if `nums[mid] == 0`, swap it with `nums[lo]` and move both `lo` and `mid` right.
If `nums[mid] == 2`, swap it with `nums[hi]` and move `hi` left — do not move `mid`, because the value swapped in has not been looked at yet.
If `nums[mid] == 1`, just move `mid` right.
approaches.why: Every step either moves `mid` right or `hi` left, shrinking the unknown region by one, so at most n steps in one pass.

trapping-rain-water.pattern: Water above a bar = min(tallest on the left, tallest on the right) − its height; two pointers make it O(1) space

approaches.name: For each bar, scan left and right for the tallest walls
approaches.idea: The water above bar `i` is limited by the tallest bar on its left and the tallest on its right: `min(leftMax, rightMax) − height[i]`. Compute both by scanning, separately for every bar.
steps: For each `i`, scan `0..i` for `leftMax` and `i..n − 1` for `rightMax` (both include `height[i]`, so the result is never negative).
Add `min(leftMax, rightMax) − height[i]` to the total.
Return the total.
approaches.why: Each of the n bars scans the whole array once. Only a few variables are kept.

approaches.name: Precompute the tallest bar on each side
approaches.idea: The brute force recomputes the same maxima again and again. Store them: `left[i]` is the tallest bar in `0..i`, `right[i]` the tallest in `i..n − 1`.
steps: Fill `left` from the left: `left[i] = max(left[i − 1], height[i])`.
Fill `right` from the right: `right[i] = max(right[i + 1], height[i])`.
Sum `min(left[i], right[i]) − height[i]` over all `i`.
approaches.why: Three linear passes; the two helper arrays take O(n) memory.

approaches.name: Monotonic stack, filling water layer by layer
approaches.idea: Keep a stack of bar indices with decreasing heights. When a taller bar arrives, the bar on top of the stack is a valley floor between the new bar and the bar below it in the stack; fill that horizontal layer.
steps: For each index `i`: while the stack is not empty and `height[i] > height[top]`, pop `floor = top`.
If the stack is now empty, there is no left wall: stop popping.
Otherwise the left wall is the new top: add `(min(height[left], height[i]) − height[floor]) × (i − left − 1)`.
Push `i` and continue; return the total.
approaches.why: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the work is O(n) in total. The stack can hold all n indices for a falling slope.

approaches.name: Two pointers with running maxima
approaches.idea: Only the smaller of the two maxima matters. If `height[l] < height[r]`, the right side already has a wall at least as tall as anything on the left so far, so the water at `l` is decided by `leftMax` alone — and the same holds mirrored.
steps: Set `l = 0`, `r = n − 1`, `leftMax = rightMax = 0`.
While `l < r`: if `height[l] < height[r]`, update `leftMax` with `height[l]`, add `leftMax − height[l]`, and move `l` right.
Otherwise update `rightMax` with `height[r]`, add `rightMax − height[r]`, and move `r` left.
Return the total.
approaches.why: One pass with each step moving one pointer. When `height[l] < height[r]`, the true right maximum for `l` is at least `height[r] > height[l]`, and `leftMax` is the true left maximum, so `min` is `leftMax` and the water at `l` is exact.

remove-element.pattern: Read and write pointers (overwrite instead of delete)

approaches.name: Shift left on every match
approaches.idea: Each time `val` is found, shift everything after it one place left, the way deleting from an array really works.
steps: Keep the current length `n`, starting at `nums.length`, and an index `i = 0`.
If `nums[i] == val`, move `nums[i + 1..n − 1]` one place left and shrink `n`; do not advance `i`, since a new value now sits there.
Otherwise advance `i`. Return `n` at the end.
approaches.why: Every removal shifts up to n values. Fine for 100 elements, but the shifting is wasted work: nothing beyond position k is checked, so the order of the tail never mattered.

approaches.name: Write index
approaches.idea: Scan once with a read index and copy every value that is not `val` to the next free slot at the front.
steps: Set the write index `w = 0`.
For each value `x` in `nums`: if `x != val`, set `nums[w] = x` and increment `w`.
Return `w`: the first `w` slots hold exactly the kept values, in their original order.
approaches.why: One pass, one write per kept value. `w` never passes the read position, so a value is always read before it can be overwritten. A variant swaps matches with the last element to do fewer writes when `val` is rare.

approaches.name: Copy into a reversed buffer
approaches.idea: Write the characters into a new array back to front, then copy them back into `s`.
steps: Create a buffer `t` of the same length.
Set `t[i] = s[n − 1 − i]` for every `i`.
Copy `t` back into `s`.
approaches.why: Linear time, but it breaks the O(1) memory rule the problem sets. Interviewers ask this question precisely to see the in-place swap.

approaches.name: Swap from both ends
approaches.idea: Swap the outermost pair, then step both pointers inwards until they meet.
steps: Set `i = 0` and `j = n − 1`.
While `i < j`, swap `s[i]` and `s[j]`, then do `i++` and `j--`.
approaches.why: n/2 swaps and two index variables. The middle character of an odd-length array is never touched, which is correct: it stays in place.

valid-palindrome-ii.pattern: Opposite-end pointers with one branch at the first mismatch

approaches.name: Try deleting each character
approaches.idea: If the string is already a palindrome, answer true. Otherwise delete each position in turn and test whether what is left is a palindrome.
steps: If `s` is a palindrome, return `true`.
For each index `k`, check whether `s` without `s[k]` is a palindrome (compare characters while skipping index `k`).
Return `true` if any deletion works, otherwise `false`.
approaches.why: n candidate deletions, each checked in O(n). With 10⁵ characters that is about 10¹⁰ steps, far too slow. The skip is done with index arithmetic so no new strings are built.

approaches.name: Two pointers, branch once
approaches.idea: Move inwards from both ends while the characters match. At the first mismatch, one of those two characters must be the one to delete, so try skipping each.
steps: Set `i = 0`, `j = n − 1`. While `i < j` and `s[i] == s[j]`, move both inwards.
If they meet, `s` is already a palindrome: return `true`.
Otherwise return whether `s[i + 1..j]` or `s[i..j − 1]` is a palindrome.
approaches.why: The outer pairs that matched stay matched whichever character is deleted, so only the two characters at the mismatch are candidates. Each of the two final checks is O(n). Trying only one side is the classic bug: in "cbbcc" the first mismatch is b against c, and only skipping the right-hand c works.

merge-strings-alternately.pattern: Two pointers walking two sequences in step

approaches.name: Concatenate strings directly
approaches.idea: Build the answer with plain string `+`, one letter at a time.
steps: Start with an empty string `out`.
For `i` from 0 to the longer length − 1, add `word1[i]` and then `word2[i]` when they exist.
Return `out`.
approaches.why: In Java and JavaScript, strings are immutable, so each `+` may copy everything built so far. With 100-letter words it is fast anyway, but it is a habit to avoid; Python and C++ handle `+=` on a growing string better.

approaches.name: Two pointers into a builder
approaches.idea: Advance one pointer in each word, appending alternately to a string builder; then append whatever is left of the longer word.
steps: Set `i = 0`, `j = 0` and an empty builder.
While both words have letters left, append `word1[i++]` then `word2[j++]`.
Append the rest of `word1` from `i` and the rest of `word2` from `j` (one of them is empty) and return the result.
approaches.why: Each letter is appended once, and a builder grows in amortised O(1) per character. The output itself needs m + n characters, so that space is unavoidable.

merge-sorted-array.pattern: Two pointers merging from the back

approaches.name: Copy in, then sort
approaches.idea: Put the values of `nums2` into the spare slots of `nums1` and sort the whole array.
steps: For each `j`, set `nums1[m + j] = nums2[j]`.
Sort `nums1`.
approaches.why: Correct and short, but it ignores that both halves are already sorted. (Library sorts may use O(log n) extra stack.) The interviewer will ask for the linear merge next.

approaches.name: Merge forwards with a copy
approaches.idea: Copy the first `m` values of `nums1` aside, then do the standard merge of two sorted lists into `nums1` from the front.
steps: Copy `nums1[0..m − 1]` into `a`.
With `i` in `a` and `j` in `nums2`, repeatedly write the smaller front value to `nums1[w++]`.
When one runs out, copy the rest of the other.
approaches.why: Linear time. The copy is needed because writing at the front would overwrite values of `nums1` that have not been merged yet.

approaches.name: Merge from the back
approaches.idea: The free space is at the end of `nums1`, so fill it from the end with the largest remaining value.
steps: Set `i = m − 1`, `j = n − 1` and `w = m + n − 1`.
While `j >= 0`: if `i >= 0` and `nums1[i] > nums2[j]`, write `nums1[i--]` to `nums1[w--]`; otherwise write `nums2[j--]`.
When `nums2` is used up, the rest of `nums1` is already in place.
approaches.why: The write position `w` always stays at or after `i` (there are `j + 1` free slots between them), so no unread value of `nums1` is overwritten. Looping only while `j >= 0` handles `m = 0` and `n = 0` naturally.

4sum.pattern: Sort, fix two values, two pointers for the last pair

approaches.name: Four nested loops with a set
approaches.idea: Sort the array, try every combination of four positions, and keep the matching quadruplets in a set so duplicates disappear.
steps: Sort `nums` so each quadruplet comes out in a canonical order.
Loop over `a < b < c < d`; if the sum (as a 64-bit value) equals `target`, add the four values to a set.
Return the set as a list.
approaches.why: With n = 200 there are about 6.6 × 10⁷ combinations of four: slow but it finishes. q is the number of answers kept in the set. The sum must be 64-bit: 4 × 10⁹ overflows a 32-bit int.

approaches.name: Three loops and a hash set for the last value
approaches.idea: Fix three values and look up the fourth in a set of values seen to the right, like Two Sum with a hash set.
steps: Sort `nums`. For each pair `a < b`, scan `c` from `b + 1` with an empty set `seen`.
If `target − nums[a] − nums[b] − nums[c]` is in `seen`, record the sorted quadruplet in a result set.
Add `nums[c]` to `seen` and continue.
approaches.why: One loop fewer than brute force, at the cost of a hash set per pair. Duplicates still need a result set; the sorted two-pointer version avoids that entirely.

approaches.name: Sort + two fixed values + two pointers
approaches.idea: After sorting, fix the first two values with nested loops and find the last two with pointers moving inwards, skipping repeated values at every level.
steps: Sort `nums`. Loop `a`, skipping a value equal to the previous `a`; inside, loop `b > a`, skipping repeats the same way.
Set `i = b + 1`, `j = n − 1`. Compute the 64-bit sum of the four values.
On a match, record it, then move `i` and `j` past any copies of their values. If the sum is too small move `i` right, if too large move `j` left.
approaches.why: O(n²) pairs times an O(n) pointer sweep. Skipping repeats at each level means every quadruplet is produced once, so no set is needed (sorting may use O(log n) stack). The same idea generalises to kSum by recursing down to the two-pointer base case.

rotate-array.pattern: In-place reversal (reverse all, then reverse each part)

approaches.name: Rotate one step, k times
approaches.idea: Move the last value to the front, shifting everything else right by one, and repeat `k % n` times.
steps: Reduce `k` to `k % n`.
Repeat `k` times: save `nums[n − 1]`, shift `nums[0..n − 2]` one place right, put the saved value at `nums[0]`.
approaches.why: Each single step costs O(n). With n and k both up to 10⁵ that is up to 10¹⁰ moves, which times out on the large test.

approaches.name: Extra array
approaches.idea: Each value at index `i` belongs at `(i + k) % n`. Place everything in a new array, then copy it back.
steps: Create `out` of length `n`.
Set `out[(i + k) % n] = nums[i]` for every `i`.
Copy `out` back into `nums`.
approaches.why: Linear time and easy to get right, but it uses a second array. The follow-up asks for O(1) extra space.

approaches.name: Three reversals
approaches.idea: Reversing the whole array puts the last `k` values at the front, but backwards. Reverse those `k` values, then reverse the rest, and both parts read forwards again.
steps: Set `k = k % n`.
Reverse `nums[0..n − 1]`.
Reverse `nums[0..k − 1]`, then reverse `nums[k..n − 1]`.
approaches.why: Each value is swapped at most twice. Example with k = 3: `[1..7]` → `[7,6,5,4,3,2,1]` → `[5,6,7,4,3,2,1]` → `[5,6,7,1,2,3,4]`. Forgetting `k % n` breaks the case k ≥ n; a cyclic-replacement method also works in O(1) space but is harder to get right.
